title: Classical fractons with cosmological fixed points
authors: Akash Singh, Dileep P. Jatkar, S. L. Sondhi, Abhishodh Prakash
abstract: Classical fractons are Hamiltonian systems that can develop attractors after projection onto configuration or shape variables, although the full phase space admits none. We study a scale-invariant, dipole-conserving two-parameter family of fracton Hamiltonians $H_{α,β}$. By separating coordinates into scale and shape, we obtain autonomous shape dynamics that admit fixed points which leave a purely scale evolution of the form $R(t)\propto |t|^{α/(α-β)}$. The shape fixed points, which determine the distribution of the expanding particles, are central configurations of power-law Riesz potentials. The distinguished model $(α,β)=(-2,1)$ is unique: its scale evolution takes the Einstein-de Sitter form $R(t)\propto |t|^{2/3}$, its fixed-point equation is the equal-mass Newtonian central-configuration, its large-$N$ distribution is a homogeneous ball, and its homothetic trajectories admit a zero-energy Newtonian gravitational dual. The fixed points are locally stable, and simulations at moderate $N$ approach them from random initial data. Large $N$ simulations reveal a richer class of fixed-points: bound clusters of approximately fixed physical size retain internal motion, while their centers approach unequal-mass Newtonian central configurations and preserve large-scale homogeneity. A scale-separation conjecture yields an effective unequal-mass fracton dynamics for the centers and a corresponding zero-energy Newtonian gravitational dual. Trajectories generically exhibit a bidirectional arrow of time: scale and shape complexity grow away from a Janus point, while Boltzmann entropy grows logarithmically. Together, these features reproduce the salient structure of a flat matter-dominated cosmology. In the distinguished fracton model, all these cosmological analogues emerge as attractor properties, making it a toy model for cosmological dynamics without fine-tuning.
summary: This paper analyzes classical fracton systems to show how complex microscopic rules can lead to simple, universal macroscopic behaviors. By projecting the system's dynamics onto scale and shape variables, the authors demonstrate that a specific model naturally reproduces the expansion law ($R(t) \propto t^{2/3}$) and other hallmarks of matter-dominated cosmology as stable attractors.
main_problem: The study investigates how complex, conservative microscopic dynamics (classical fractons) can robustly generate simple, universal late-time behaviors characteristic of cosmology.
main_result: For the distinguished model $(\alpha,  eta) = (-2, 1)$, the system's reduced dynamics exhibit attractor properties that reproduce key features of flat matter-dominated cosmology without fine-tuning.
method: The methodology involves separating coordinates into scale and shape to derive autonomous dynamics, followed by stability analysis using Jacobian projections and calculating the Boltzmann entropy in the reduced phase space.
model_or_system: The system is classical fractons, described by a scale-invariant, dipole-conserving Hamiltonian $H_{\alpha, eta}$. The dynamics are analyzed after projecting the full phase space onto configuration or shape variables to find stable attractors.
key_observables: Scale evolution $R(t) \propto |t|^{\alpha/(\alpha- eta)}$, fixed points (central configurations of Riesz potentials), and the Boltzmann entropy $S_B \propto \log ( ar{R}/R^*)$.
important_parameters: The parameters $(\alpha,  eta)$, especially the distinguished case $(-2, 1)$ which yields the Einstein-de Sitter exponent $2/3$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on projecting the full Hamiltonian onto reduced shape variables to obtain attractor dynamics in the lower-dimensional space.
figures_summary: Not specified (Notes mention figures showing separation evolution approaching the 2/3 slope for N=256 and N=1000).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the fracton Hamiltonian, separating coordinates to find autonomous shape dynamics, analyzing fixed point stability via Jacobian projection, calculating the reduced Boltzmann entropy, and finally demonstrating the cosmological analogy in the distinguished limit.
why_interesting: It provides a non-standard, purely classical mechanical framework (fractons) that yields emergent cosmological behavior, offering an alternative theoretical playground for understanding late-time universe dynamics without relying on standard fine-tuning assumptions.

Figure 2: Large-N regular isotropic shape densities. The filled-ball configuration has the radial density in Theorem 1; the special point q = −1 is a homogeneous solid ball, while q = 1 is the condensation point to a uniform spherical shell.

Figure 3: Eigenvalue spectra of the reduced Jacobian for N = 75 fixed points correspond- ing to three representative central configurations: a collinear saddle, the global minimum, and a planar saddle. The top row corresponds to the expanding branch, while the bottom row shows the corresponding contracting branch. The minimum and maximum real parts of the eigenvalue spectrum are indicated in each panel. Stable and unstable eigenvalues are denoted by circles and triangles, respectively.

Figure 4: Evolution of N = 25 particles with shape phase-space {si, ui} initializations selected from a Gaussian random number generator with mean 0 and variance 1 but then re-centered and re-scaled to satisfy constraints Eq. The inset shows the scale R(t) settling into expansion for each seed, hence showing that the expanding branch is dynamically selected.
